title: Kumbhakarna's sleep
hookLine: a giant opens his mouth to ask the Creator for a boon, and what comes out is: let me sleep
carry: too much sleep is tamas, not yoga
tomorrow: why make a resolve before you rest?

lines: THE GODDESS OF SPEECH IN HIS MOUTH.
cards: Three brothers do fierce austerities, and Brahma, the Creator, comes to grant each a boon. One is Ravana. One is Vibhishana.
The third is Kumbhakarna, a giant so huge and so hungry that the gods are terrified of what he'll ask for.

So, in the Ramayana's telling, Brahma calls on Sarasvati, the goddess of speech, and she slips into the giant's mouth. Kumbhakarna opens it to ask his boon, and what comes out is: let me sleep for many years. And he does.

teach.h: HE MEANT A THRONE. HE ASKED FOR SLEEP.
teach.b: A well-loved retelling makes it a slip of the tongue: he meant to ask for indrasana, Indra's throne, and said nidrasana, a bed of sleep. Brahma softens the boon only a little: six months asleep, one day awake.
When Rama's army reaches Lanka, it takes drums, shouting and elephants to wake him. He tells Ravana plainly that he's in the wrong, then fights for his brother anyway, and falls.
To this day Hindu families tease a late sleeper by calling him Kumbhakarna. Now set him beside Vishnu, three days ago, asleep on the waters. Two sleepers, two kinds of sleep.
Vishnu's is yoga nidra, held by the Goddess, and he rises the moment she lets him go. Kumbhakarna's is heaviness, a sleep that swallows most of a life.
The Gita has a name for that heaviness: tamas, the quality of dullness, which, Krishna says, binds a person through carelessness, laziness and sleep.

teach.h: NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE.
teach.b: And in chapter six he says yoga isn't for one who sleeps too much, or for one who never sleeps; it's for one moderate in sleep and in waking. Patanjali adds a sober note.

teach.h: SLEEP IS STILL A MOVEMENT OF THE MIND.
teach.b: In the Yoga Sutras he lists five movements of the mind, the vrittis, and sleep is one: the movement that rests on the experience of absence. Deep sleep isn't stillness.
Some commentators point to the morning: we wake and say, I slept well, I knew nothing. Something registered that nothing. So drifting off isn't yoga.
Rest with someone awake inside it is: Vishnu's kind, not Kumbhakarna's.

how: Hindu families retell Kumbhakarna's sleep from the Ramayana, often to tease a late riser; students of the Gita and the Yoga Sutras read Gita 6.16–17 and 14.8 on sleep and tamas, and Yoga Sutra 1.10 on sleep as a movement of the mind.

games.q: two sleepers this week: Vishnu on the waters, Kumbhakarna in Lanka. which sleep is the Gita warning about?
o: Vishnu's. a god shouldn't sleep at all.
Kumbhakarna's: heavy, too much, the binding of tamas.
neither. all sleep is the same.
games.why: Gita 14.8 says tamas binds through carelessness, laziness and sleep, and 6.16 says yoga isn't for one who sleeps too much, or too little.

practice: Lie down or sit back and let the body grow heavy, and when a wave of drowsiness comes, notice it as a movement, the way you'd notice a thought: heaviness arriving, heaviness passing.
If you begin to drift, don't fight it hard; come back to the breath at the nose, then watch the heaviness return. Resting and watching, both at once.

wordCard.voice: Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga: rest with awareness inside it. Vishnu's sleep, not Kumbhakarna's.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: nidra, sleep. In Yoga Sutra 1.10, one of the five movements of the mind.

carryVoice: Your line: too much sleep is tamas, not yoga. Vishnu rests and rises; Kumbhakarna just sleeps. See you tomorrow.
